hints: List the ions present from saturated $\text{KCl(aq)}$ and water, then compare ease of discharge at each electrode considering concentration and reactivity.
walkthrough:
Sort out the competing ions**
You have $\text{K}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ from the salt, plus $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ from water. At the cathode cations compete, at the anode anions compete. Remember the cathode is negative so attracts cations, the anode is positive so attracts anions.

Apply concentration and reactivity rules**
At the cathode $\text{K}^{+}$ is a very reactive metal ion and stays in solution, so $\text{H}^{+}$ from water is discharged as $\text{H}_{2}$. At the anode the solution is saturated, so the high $[\text{Cl}^{-}]$ favours discharge of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ over $\text{OH}^{-}$, giving $\text{Cl}_{2}$.

Final answer: at the anode: chlorine, $\text{Cl}_{2}$
at the cathode: hydrogen, $\text{H}_{2}$

hints: Start with charge passed using $Q = It$ and remember to convert 15.0 minutes into seconds.
Convert charge into moles of electrons using $n(e^{-}) = Q/F$ with $F = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}$.

Link electrons to oxygen using the anode half equation $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_{2} + 4\text{H}^{+} + 4e^{-}$ and then use $24000\text{ cm}^{3}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ for room conditions.
walkthrough:
Find the total charge**
Charge is current multiplied by time in seconds:
$$Q = It$$
$$Q = 0.750 \times 15.0 \times 60 = 675\text{ C}$$
Always convert minutes to seconds first, a classic place to lose marks.

Convert charge to moles of electrons**
One mole of electrons carries $96500\text{ C}$:
$$n(e^{-}) = \frac{Q}{F} = \frac{675}{96500} = 7.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$$
This tells you how many electrons were pushed round the circuit.

Use the anode stoichiometry to get oxygen**
Oxygen from acidified water comes from:
$$2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_{2} + 4\text{H}^{+} + 4e^{-}$$
So 4 moles of $e^{-}$ make 1 mole of $\text{O}_{2}$:
$$n(\text{O}_{2}) = \frac{7.0 \times 10^{-3}}{4} = 1.75 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$$
$$V = n \times 24000 = 1.75 \times 10^{-3} \times 24000 = 42.0\text{ cm}^{3}$$

hints: Recall the $E^{\ominus}$ values for $\text{X}_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{X}^{-}$ from the Data Booklet and how they change from chlorine to iodine.
walkthrough:
Read the halogen oxidant couples**
For oxidising action you need $\text{X}_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{X}^{-}$. From the Data Booklet the values fall down the group: $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is $+1.36\text{ V}$, $\text{Br}_{2}$ is $+1.07\text{ V}$, $\text{I}_{2}$ is $+0.54\text{ V}$. More positive means stronger oxidant, so chlorine is strongest.
Final answer: $\text{Cl}_{2}/\text{Cl}^{-}$ $+1.36\text{ V}$; $\text{Br}_{2}/\text{Br}^{-}$ $+1.07\text{ V}$; $\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}$ $+0.54\text{ V}$

hints: Compare each halogen $E^{\ominus}$ value with $E^{\ominus}(\text{Sn}^{4+}/\text{Sn}^{2+}) = +0.15\text{ V}$ to see which gives a positive $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$.
Recall that a reaction is feasible under standard conditions when $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode} > 0$.
Think how to combine $\text{X}_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{X}^{-}$ with $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^{-}$ to write the overall ionic equation.
walkthrough:
Set up the cell logic**
Think of $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ being oxidised to $\text{Sn}^{4+}$:
$$\text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Sn}^{2+} \quad E^{\ominus} = +0.15\text{ V}$$
The halogen is reduced. Feasibility needs:
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}(\text{halogen}) - E^{\ominus}(\text{Sn}^{4+}/\text{Sn}^{2+}) > 0$$

Check all three halogens**
Even the weakest oxidant iodine at $+0.54\text{ V}$ is still well above $+0.15\text{ V}$:
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 0.54 - 0.15 = +0.39\text{ V}$$
For bromine it is $+0.92\text{ V}$ and for chlorine $+1.21\text{ V}$. All positive, so all three oxidise $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ under standard conditions.

Write the combined equation**
Add reduction and oxidation, electrons cancel:
$$\text{X}_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{X}^{-}$$
$$\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^{-}$$
Giving:
$$\text{Sn}^{2+} + \text{X}_{2} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{X}^{-}$$

Final answer: All three halogens, chlorine, bromine and iodine, will react.
All halogen $E^{\ominus}$ values (+1.36, +1.07, +0.54 V) are more positive than $E^{\ominus}(\text{Sn}^{4+}/\text{Sn}^{2+}) = +0.15\text{ V}$, so $E^{\ominus}_{cell} > 0$ in each case.
E.g. $\text{Sn}^{2+} + \text{X}_{2} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{X}^{-}$ where $\text{X} = \text{Cl, Br, I}$

hints: Compare $E^{\ominus}(\text{Cl}_{2}/\text{Cl}^{-}) = +1.36\text{ V}$ with the couples $\text{MnO}_{2}/\text{Mn}^{2+} (+1.23\text{ V})$ and $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{Mn}^{2+} (+1.52\text{ V})$ to see which oxidation is feasible.
walkthrough:
See how far chlorine can oxidise manganese**
Chlorine at $+1.36\text{ V}$ is strong enough to oxidise $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ to $\text{MnO}_{2}$ ($+1.23\text{ V}$) because $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 1.36 - 1.23 > 0$. It is not strong enough to reach $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ ($+1.52\text{ V}$) because that would give a negative $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$. So oxidation stops at $\text{MnO}_{2}$.

hints: Identify the more positive half cell ($\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}/\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$, $+2.01\text{ V}$) as the cathode and subtract $E^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Subtract the right way round**
The peroxodisulfate couple is much more positive, so it is reduced while $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is oxidised:
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$$
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 2.01 - 0.77 = 1.24\text{ V}$$
Final answer: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 2.01 - 0.77 = +1.24\text{ V}$

hints: Notice both half cells contain only ions in solution with no solid metal to act as an electron conductor.
walkthrough:
Choose an inert conductor**
Neither half cell provides its own metal electrode, both are ion to ion systems. You need an inert surface to transfer electrons without reacting, so use platinum (unreactive and conducts) in each half cell.
Final answer: platinum in the $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ half-cell and platinum in the $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}/\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ half-cell

hints: Think which concentration changes push each equilibrium toward greater tendency for the actual cell reaction ($\text{Fe}^{2+}$ oxidised, $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}$ reduced) to increase $E_{cell}$.
walkthrough:
Shift each half cell to make the cell more powerful**
The cell reaction oxidises $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and reduces $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}$ to $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$. By Le Chatelier, adding reactant or removing product drives that half reaction forward. So raise $[\text{Fe}^{2+}]$ or lower $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ to make the iron half cell more easily oxidised (more negative), and raise $[\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}]$ or lower $[\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}]$ to make the peroxodisulfate half cell more easily reduced (more positive). Both changes widen the gap and increase $E_{cell}$.

Final answer: $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ half-cell: increase $[\text{Fe}^{2+}]$ or decrease $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$; $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}/\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ half-cell: increase $[\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}]$ or decrease $[\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}]$
